Photograph: Kent Nishimura/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images US news AOC refuses to rule out run against Senate leader Chuck Schumer ‘I’ll cross that bridge when I get to it,’ the progressive US representative says US politics live – latest updates Ariana Baio Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.23 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez , the progressive Democratic congresswoman, has refused to rule out a potential run against the party’s Senate leader Chuck Schumer amid mounting speculation around her political ambitions. When asked by the New York Times whether she would challenge Schumer in 2028, when his current term is up, Ocasio-Cortez declined to exclude the possibility – even if Democrats win back the Senate majority. “We’re working hard to have that problem,” Ocasio-Cortez, 36, told the newspaper of a Democratic majority in the Senate, which she called called “the best possible problem we could have as a country”, adding: “And I’ll cross that bridge when I get to it.” The New York congresswoman emphasized that any decision she makes would be personal, saying: “I don’t think that my decisions would come down to deference.” Ocasio-Cortez has been repeatedly cited as a potential challenger to Schumer, 75, an even a Democratic presidential candidate in 2028. She has built a significant profile since defeating a top incumbent Democrat to win her seat in the House of Representatives, representing an area of New York City, in 2018. Her progressive policies have resonated with younger Democrats, women and Hispanic voters, according to recent polling from the New York Times/Siena University . She has become a leading figure in rallying anti- Donald Trump voters. She has also raised more money than many of her House colleagues, securing more than $32m since 2025. As of June 2026, Ocasio-Cortez had more than $15m in cash, according to Federal Election Commission data. But Ocasio-Cortez is also polarizing, with roughly 41% of likely voters and 75% of Republicans finding her unfavorable. That combination has made her an easy target for Republican attacks, particularly from the US president. Though her name is floated as a potential 2028 presidential contender, Ocasio-Cortez has been elusive about her plans, often leaving the door open to a run while acknowledging the hurdles she faces. “I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina,” Ocasio-Cortez told the New York Times. “And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities.” Taking on Schumer could be Ocasio-Cortez’s first step to fulfilling greater political ambitions. Earlier this year, a survey from the liberal firm Data for Progress found that 55% of likely Democratic voters said they would support or lean toward supporting Ocasio-Cortez, while only 36% would back Schumer. https://www.politico.eu/article/5-things.text: LONDON — Britain’s government runs on numbers — but what if they’re a shot in the dark? From tepid economic growth to squeezed household incomes, this week’s budget from Chancellor John Healey was packed with grim figures about the state of play in the U.K. — and a host of costly measures to try and turn things around. Yet it’s almost certain that the budget forecasts Healey relied upon Wednesday will be revised by the time the next fiscal event rolls around. Advertisement Advertisement In this week’s episode of the Westminster Insider podcast , POLITICO unpacked the numbers that govern the U.K. — and found out just how many doubts there are about the information the country relies on. 1. True levels of immigration Few issues divide Brits like immigration — but grappling with hard data on the issue has proven to be a repeated challenge to governments of all stripes. For decades, immigration into the U.K. was calculated by the International Passenger Survey (IPS) — essentially people with clipboards at airports, train stations and ports asking people about their intention to stay in the U.K. The Eurostar platform is pictured at St. Pancras station in London on Nov. 14, 2007. | Cate Gillon/Getty Images But between 2012 and 2020, the number of European Union nationals coming into the country was off by 76% — or 93,000 people a year. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) only discovered this error after trialing a new approach to counting immigration that focused less heavily on the IPS, which was dropped altogether in 2025. The ONS now uses this new measurement — relying on a combination of Home Office data, information from the Department for Work and Pensions and tax receipts. But this was again wrong in the year to June 2023 — by 234,000 people. Advertisement Advertisement The original numbers published by the ONS in November 2023 said net migration to the U.K. was 672,000. A year later, the ONS admitted there had been a mistake and said it was in fact 906,000. Laura Gilbert, who ran data science in No. 10 Downing Street until last year, told POLITICO that net migration numbers are often incredibly misleading — and even the way we calculate those numbers is “highly spurious.” Gilbert says the quality of the numbers on immigration normally improves months later, sometimes by “quite a lot.” But she warned, “if politicians are making a decision based on exact numbers, often they are using the first number that comes out, which is the worst one.” 2. The scale of unemployment Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have vowed to get welfare spending down “but in a Labour way.” Much of this will rest on getting young people into work, the subject of a 217-page report by Tony Blair-era minister Alan Milburn. But Britain’s workforce — and the number of young people out of work — is counted by the Labour Force Survey (LFS), an ONS measurement beset with issues. For example, between 2019 and 2024, the LFS missed 1 million workers because people with full-time jobs are less likely to answer the phone to surveyors during the week, according to the Resolution Foundation think tank. Advertisement Advertisement The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) admitted just this week that the survey is too unreliable to measure productivity. “In recent years, falling response rates have significantly affected the quality of the LFS, making it more difficult to estimate reliably the number of workers and the hours they work,” the watchdog said. Gilbert says Healey’s claim that there are “1 million young people out of work” is unlikely to be accurate. The number of NEETs — people not in education, employment or training — is also based on figures from a subset of the LFS, which is particularly susceptible to inaccuracies. Healey leaves No. 11 Downing St. in London to present the budget to Parliament on Oct. 28, 2026. | Peter Nicholls/Getty Images “I think being within 50,000 on either side of that number is very unlikely to be the sort of level of accuracy that you’re at,” Gilbert said. “It’s entirely spurious, if I’m completely honest, but it’s a big number, you write it down, and everyone reads the papers.” Ben Warner, who set up 10DS, Downing Street’s data science unit, says the LFS can’t accurately measure the number of entrepreneurs arriving in the country, either, making it difficult for ministers to know if decisions — such as a much-hyped tax relief for founders — are actually encouraging people to come to the U.K. “I’m willing to bet you a hundred quid [we don’t have accurate numbers] at the level that you would need to make thoughtful policy around this,” Warner said. “I am sure there are people who have very, very good knowledge of the economic statistics. But if you’re a minister, you don’t necessarily have access.” Advertisement Advertisement 3. Where inflation and GDP sit These are hugely important measures for a government: Are costs rising for households — and is the British economy growing? But buried inside this week’s budget assessment by the OBR was a startling admission: There is a one in five chance inflation in 2027 will come in at over 4.5% … and the same chance it will be under 2.5%. They are profoundly different outcomes for the cost of living, a top political issue. Warner told POLITICO, “The whole thing is mental. We are discussing the uncertainty of the numbers and pretending that these are real.” Gilbert says there are knock-on effects at play: problems with net migration numbers and workforce data bleed into inflation and GDP projections. “Understanding migration tells us about the demographics of the country, and when we look at how many people are in work, and that is wildly undercounted, it looks like there are more people who are unemployed, which has a knock-on effect on GDP and inflation,” she explained. 4. The number of kids on free school meals The number of pupils in England on free school meals is just over 2.2 million, according to government statistics from the start of this year. That’s more than a quarter of all children in the country. Advertisement Advertisement But Gilbert warns that these numbers are likely to be overestimated because schools “game the system” when census data is collected. “So for anyone who has children in school they may have received a text message that says don’t send them to school with a packed lunch — because the schools get funding based on how many children are on school meals,” she said. 5. The number of rough sleepers on the streets One of Burnham’s flagship promises when he became prime minister was to end homelessness in the U.K., and Wednesday’s budget put £432 million towards precisely that promise. Yet the way rough sleepers are counted in the U.K. varies according to each council, with some areas relying on an estimate and others on a street count — sending workers out to physically count the number of people on the streets on a particular day in autumn. Tents line the side of Euston Road in London on Nov. 13, 2025. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Some councils have swapped between methods — which can make it look as though they have dramatically reduced their rough sleepers from one year to the next. For example, in 2017 Brighton and Hove Council used an estimate of rough sleepers which put that number at 176. The following year, the council used a street count — but this took place on a snowy night, so the number fell to 68. This made it appear as though the number of people experiencing homelessness had been more than halved. Advertisement
